title: How infused oils work
subtitle: A practical guide to herbal oil infusions
excerpt: What herbal infused oils are, how they differ from essential oils, how to make them by two methods, which herbs suit which method, and how to know when the oil is ready. The reference article for readers making calendula oil, St John's wort oil, rosemary oil, and similar preparations.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931) : oil preparations described throughout, including St John's wort and calendula. British Herbal Pharmacopoeia (1983) : infused oil preparations, ratio and method guidance. EMA HMPC monographs on Calendula officinalis and Hypericum perforatum : oil preparations referenced in traditional-use assessments. Oil stability and rancidity notes synthesised from general food-oil chemistry: olive, sweet almond, and sunflower are widely used in herbal practice and their comparative stability is well documented.

glossaryTerms.definition: A carrier oil that has been gently heated or cold-infused with dried plant material to draw out fat-soluble constituents. Different from an essential oil, which is a steam-distilled concentrate.

A plant-based oil used as the base in an infused oil or topical preparation. Common examples are olive, sweet almond, and sunflower. Called a carrier because it carries the plant's constituents onto the skin.

A slow, cool method of infusing plant material into oil using natural warmth from a sunny windowsill over four to six weeks. The plant releases its constituents gradually into the oil without the use of external heat.

content.text: Herbal infused oils: what they are, how they are made, and how to know when one is done. This article is the reference guide for anyone making an oil-based herbal preparation, whether that is a calendula oil for skin care, a St John's wort oil for nerve pain, a rosemary oil for aching muscles, or a comfrey oil that will later become a salve. After reading it, you will know which method to use for which herb, what to look and smell for, and how to store the finished oil.

This publication does not offer medical advice. If you are using a herbal oil for a health purpose, read the individual remedy page for that herb. Which carries the safety information, dosing guidance, and any drug-effect notes that apply to your specific preparation
What an infused oil is
An
infused oil
is a
carrier oil

that has been infused with the fat-soluble active compounds of a plant. You pack a plant into a jar of oil, give it time (or gentle heat), and the oil draws out the plant's oil-soluble compounds. The result is a lightly coloured, scented oil that carries some of the plant's character.

An infused oil is not the same as an essential oil. An essential oil is a concentrated steam distillate of the plant's volatile compounds, produced by specialist distillation equipment. A herbal infused oil is a home preparation: the plant material steeps in a carrier oil. The result is gentler and lower concentration than an essential oil, but it is also far easier to prepare, safer to use on the skin, and appropriate for a much wider range of people.
The standard ratio

One part dried herb to five parts oil, by weight. This is the ratio used in the individual remedy pages on this site. Weigh the herb first, then multiply by five for the oil. A 40 g batch of dried calendula flowers takes 200 ml of olive oil.

The herb must be dried, not fresh. Fresh plant material contains water, and water in oil creates conditions for mould. Even herb that feels dry can hold enough moisture to cause problems; if in doubt, spread the herb on a tray in a warm kitchen for a day before using.
Choosing your carrier oil
The carrier oil you choose affects the shelf life, the feel on the skin, and to a lesser extent the extraction. Three oils are used most often in herbal practice.

Olive oil is the traditional choice. It is stable, widely available, and skin-friendly. The flavour and scent are stronger than other options, which some people dislike in a body oil. Light or extra-light olive oil has a milder scent and is more neutral for skin preparations.

Sweet almond oil is mild in scent, absorbs well into the skin, and is popular for facial and baby preparations. It is less stable than olive oil and has a shorter shelf life (around 12 months). Avoid if the user has a tree-nut allergy.

Sunflower oil (cold-pressed, high-oleic) is light, neutral in scent, and absorbs quickly. It is the most economical option and works well for large batches. Standard supermarket sunflower oil is higher in linoleic acid and goes rancid faster; high-oleic varieties are more stable.
Two methods
Warm double-boiler method

Pack the herb and oil into a heatproof bowl set over a saucepan of simmering water. Hold the oil temperature between 60 and 65 degrees Celsius, using a probe thermometer to check. Infuse for two to four hours, stirring occasionally. Strain through muslin when done. This method is faster and useful when you need the oil within a day. It is the standard method for most herbs: calendula, rosemary, lavender, chamomile.

Temperature is the main failure mode. Too cool (below 55 degrees Celsius) and the extraction is slow and incomplete. Too hot (above 70 degrees Celsius) and you degrade the volatile active compounds you want in the oil. Use a thermometer and keep the simmering water low.
Cool solar-infusion method

Pack the herb into a glass jar, cover with oil, seal tightly, and place in a south-facing sunny window for four to six weeks. The gentle warmth of the window and natural light slowly draw out the active compounds. Shake or tilt the jar every day or two to keep the herb moving. Strain when done.
The
solar infusion

is the traditional method and is particularly suited to St John's wort oil, where the slow infusion produces the characteristic deep red colour from the hypericin in the flowers. It is also the simplest method: no heat, no thermometer, no active monitoring. The trade-off is time.
Which method for which herb
Most herbs work well with either method. Some are better suited to one:

St John's wort: traditionally solar-infused. The slow cool method is thought to produce a more complete extraction of the red hypericin pigment. Both methods work, but the solar path produces the most vivid colour.
Calendula: works well with the warm double-boiler method. The flowers are not volatile-oil-heavy and benefit from the warmth of the double-boiler extraction. The resulting oil is deep gold.
Lavender, rosemary, chamomile: both methods work. For a preparation you need within a day, use the double boiler. For a preparation that can wait six weeks, either path gives good results.
Comfrey: the warm double-boiler method is standard for comfrey oil before it is made into a salve. Note that comfrey preparations are for external use only.
How to know when the oil is ready
Two senses tell you whether the infusion has worked: smell and colour.

Smell: the finished oil should smell strongly of the herb. Hold a spoonful under your nose. If it smells mainly of the carrier oil with only a faint herbal note, the infusion is not complete or the herb was stale. If it smells clearly and strongly of the herb, it is ready.

Colour: most infused oils take on a noticeable colour shift from the carrier oil. Calendula turns the oil a warm gold. St John's wort turns it pink, then deep red over six weeks. Comfrey produces a dark green. Lavender and rosemary give a slightly deeper hue. If the colour is unchanged, the extraction has not occurred or the herb was too old.
Straining

Line a sieve with a double layer of muslin over a clean jug. Pour the infused oil and herb through and press the spent herb firmly with a wooden spoon or your hand (wearing gloves) to extract as much oil as possible. The spent herb goes in the compost. The strained oil goes through a small funnel into clean, dry amber glass bottles.

The oil must be dry, meaning no water introduced from the muslin or the jug. Squeeze the muslin firmly over the jar to drain the last of the oil, but do not allow water from damp equipment to contaminate it. Any water in the finished oil shortens shelf life dramatically.
Storage and shelf life

Store infused oils in amber glass bottles with tight-fitting lids, in a cool, dark cupboard away from heat and direct light. A well-made olive-oil-based infusion keeps for 12 months from the strain date. Sweet almond oil keeps around 12 months; it goes rancid faster in warmth. Sunflower oil (high-oleic) keeps around 12 months.

Check the oil periodically. Rancid oil smells sharp, sour, or like crayons. Any change from the fresh herbal scent to an off, stale, or sour smell means the oil has gone rancid and should be discarded. Do not use rancid oil on the skin.
Common failure modes
Cloudy oil or mould: moisture in the herb. Use properly dried herb, and ensure all equipment is dry before use.
Weak colour or scent: stale herb (more than 12 months old), or too little herb for the amount of oil, or too short an infusion time.
Burnt or cooked smell: temperature too high during the double-boiler infusion. Discard and start again.
Rancid smell before the stated shelf life: the oil was stored in warmth or light, or the original carrier oil was past its use-by date when you started.
